extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of architecture, architectural historians, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical definition and evaluative framework for 'Gothic' architecture: isolates its internal (mental) tendencies and external (material) forms, and offers criteria for judging how Gothic a building is. Also classifies types of ornamentation (servile/constitutional/revolutionary) and criticizes Renaissance tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothicness as a degree/character
rubrics_metrics.description: All we have to reason upon is merely ... a greater or less degree of Gothicness in each building we examine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gothic is not an absolute binary; buildings possess Gothic character to varying extents. Evaluation should treat 'Gothicness' as a measurable character (more or less Gothic) rather than a strict category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of both mental elements and material forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless both the elements and the forms are there, we have no right to call the style Gothic. It is not enough that it has the Form, if it have not also the power and life. It is not enough that it has the Power, if it have not the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify as Gothic a work must exhibit both internal mental tendencies (e.g., 'savagness', 'love of change') and external architectural forms (e.g., pointed arches). Possession of only one aspect makes a building only partially Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental power / expression (internal elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Its elements are certain mental tendencies of the builders, legibly expressed in it; as fancifulness, love of variety, love of richness, and such others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis should identify the builder's mental tendencies manifested in the work — these internal qualities are as crucial as external forms to the Gothic character. Both must be considered when judging style authenticity and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savageness (Gothic element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Savageness (also called Rudeness) — the rude and wild character associated with Northern origins; a quality of sternness and rugged power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Savageness is not a reproach but a noble attribute: it indicates rugged strength and religious seriousness and should be admired rather than condemned. When evaluating Gothic work, value rough majesty and robust, unpolished expression rather than dismissing imperfection as mere barbarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changefulness / Love of Change
rubrics_metrics.description: Changefulness (Love of Change) — listed as one of the characteristic mental elements of Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buildings should be assessed for dynamism, variety, and a love of altering forms and surfaces; presence of changefulness contributes to Gothicness even if other elements are partial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism / Love of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalism (Love of Nature) — one of the mental elements that constitute the Gothic soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the extent to which a building expresses natural forms, organic motifs, or a fidelity to nature's irregularities as part of its Gothic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesqueness / Disturbed Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesqueness (Disturbed Imagination) — listed among the mental characters of Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess use of fantastical, distorted, or startling sculptural elements and imagination that departs from classical restraint; grotesqueness, properly balanced, is a Gothic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity / Obstinacy (Eigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eigidity (printed in the source; interpreted as Rigidity or Obstinacy) — one of the moral elements of Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the presence of stubbornness or uncompromising structural/expressive tendencies in the work; such obstinacy supports Gothic identity even when it yields roughness or formal hardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundance / Generosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundance (Generosity) — the sixth listed characteristic; generosity as an attribute of Gothic builders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for abundant, copious ornament and largesse of design; an expansive, generous use of materials and forms is part of the Gothic spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: External material forms of Gothic
rubrics_metrics.description: External forms are pointed arches, vaulted roofs, flying buttresses, grotesque sculptures, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying Gothic style, note the material/visual signs — pointed arches, vaulting, buttressing, sculptural grotesques — but do not rely on these alone. Forms must be animated by the mental elements described above to be genuinely Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servile ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Servile ornament: execution or power of the inferior workman is entirely subjected to the intellect of the higher (examples: Greek, Ninevite, Egyptian schools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Servile ornament favors geometrical, perfectly repeatable forms executed to exact standards by subordinates. Use this category to evaluate ornament systems that prioritize mechanical perfection and symmetry and subordinate individual executor creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional ornament: the executive inferior power is, to a certain point, emancipated and independent, yet confesses its inferiority and renders obedience to higher powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify ornament systems where lower craftsmen have some creative agency within limits — produces variety and individuality while still respecting a higher design order; this is characteristic of medieval/Christian ornament practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutionary ornament: no executive inferiority is admitted at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this category for ornament where the executor's power is sovereign — ornament becomes wild, unregulated, or entirely independent of imposed higher design; recognize it as a distinct ornamental mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medieval/Christian ornament ethic (valuation of imperfection)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the mediaeval, or especially Christian, system of ornament, slavery is done away with; Christianity recognizes the individual value of every soul and confesses imperfection, bestowing dignity upon the acknowledgment of unworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate medieval/Christian works positively for their celebration of individual craftsmanship and honest imperfection. The ethical stance — valuing imperfect human expression rather than enforcing mechanical perfection — is itself an evaluative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renaissance ornament as negative tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Renaissance ornament: the inferior detail becomes principal, the executor required to exhibit skill as great as the master, overwhelming original power and making the building a 'wearisome exhibition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Renaissance tendencies critically: when detailing and executor-skill displace the master's expressive power, the result is an impoverishment of style. Use this as a cautionary criterion when judging ornamentation that overvalues polished execution at the expense of spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value individual thought/creative effort over mechanical perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not prefer smooth minuteness above shattered majesty; prize and honor the thoughtful part of manual workers even if accompanied by faults; the best in a man manifests with much error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation, prefer works that manifest individual thought and imaginative striving, even when imperfectly executed, over flawlessly produced but soulless craft. This principle should guide assessments of workmanship and ornament.
